theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Your team is given a cutting list for a steel stair frame. Explain how you would plan the cutting: grouping parts, fitting them onto stock lengths, choosing machines, allowing for saw cuts, sharing the work and recording offcuts. Include a short worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the cutting list against the drawing and revision, then group the parts by section and material, for example all the 100 × 50 channel, all the 50 × 50 angle and all the flat bar. For each group I fit the parts onto stock lengths so that waste is low, putting the longest parts first and filling the gaps with shorter ones, and allowing a few millimetres to square the first end and the kerf for every cut. For example, from a 6 m length I can cut three stringer pieces of 1950 mm with 3 mm cuts: 3 × 1953 = 5859 mm, leaving about 141 mm. I choose the machine for each group: the cold saw or bandsaw for sections and mitres, the guillotine for plate blanks. I give each team member a group and a copy of the plan, with one person checking first-off parts. Parts are marked with their part number as they are cut. Useful offcuts are labelled with size and grade and entered in the offcut register, and the rest go to sorted scrap.
markingPoints: Checks the list against the drawing; groups parts by section and material
Fits parts onto stock lengths, longest first, allowing for squaring and kerf
Gives a correct worked example
Chooses suitable machines and shares the work, with a checker
Marks parts and records useful offcuts

essays.stem: Compare sawing (bandsaw or cold saw), abrasive cutting, shearing and punching as ways of cutting steel. For each, say what work it suits, the quality of the edge, and its limits.
essays.modelAnswer: Bandsaws and cold saws cut bar, tube and sections accurately and square, at set angles, with a small kerf and little heat. They give a clean edge with a small burr. They are slower than shearing and need the right blade, speed and coolant. Abrasive cut-off saws are cheap and quick to set up and can cut hardened material, but they make heat, sparks, dust and noise, leave a heat-tinted edge with a heavy burr, and wear their discs fast. Shearing on a guillotine or ironworker cuts sheet, plate, flat bar and angle very quickly with no kerf or swarf. The edge has a rolled side and a burr, and narrow strips may twist; each machine has a limit on thickness and length, lower for stainless steel. Punching makes holes and notches very fast, with no swarf other than the slug. It needs a large force, the hole should be no smaller than the plate thickness, and the hole edge can be work-hardened and slightly tapered, so some structural specifications do not allow it on thick plate.
markingPoints: Sawing: accurate, square, angles; clean edge; slower, needs blade and coolant
Abrasive: quick, cuts hard material; heat, burr, sparks, dust, noise
Shearing: fast, no kerf; rolled edge and burr; thickness limits, twist
Punching: fast holes; large force, minimum hole size, hardened edge
Makes a sensible comparison between them

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the force needed to punch a hole, with a worked example, and why the machine's rated capacity and the minimum hole size must be checked.
essays.modelAnswer: When a hole is punched, the metal is sheared round the edge of the hole. The area being sheared is the hole's circumference times the plate thickness, so the force is: force = π × d × t × shear strength. For example, for an 18 mm hole in 8 mm mild steel with a shear strength of about 300 N/mm², the force is 3.142 × 18 × 8 × 300 = about 135 700 N, which is about 136 kN (roughly 14 tonnes). This must be less than the punching capacity on the machine's plate or in the maker's chart, for that material. Stainless steel and higher-strength steels have a higher shear strength, so they need more force. If the force is too high, the punch, die or machine frame can break and parts can fly out. The hole diameter should usually be no smaller than the plate thickness, because a small punch pushing through thick plate is likely to buckle or snap. The punch and die must also match, with the right clearance for the thickness.
markingPoints: Explains that the edge of the hole is sheared (circumference × thickness)
States force = π × d × t × shear strength
Gives a correct worked example with units
Checks the force against the machine's rated capacity for that material
Minimum hole size and matching punch and die, with the risk if ignored

essays.stem: Explain how guillotine blade clearance, rake and hold-downs affect the quality of a sheared edge, and what a team leader checks before a production run.
essays.modelAnswer: The blade clearance is the small gap between the top and bottom blades. If it is right for the material and thickness, the edge is clean, with a small burr. If it is too large, the metal tears and is dragged into the gap, giving a rough edge and a large burr, and thin sheet may jam. If it is too small, the blades rub, wear fast and the machine is overloaded. The rake is the slope of the top blade along its length. More rake lowers the cutting force, but it can twist and bow narrow strips. The hold-downs clamp the sheet before the blade cuts; if they are not working the sheet moves, giving an out-of-square cut and a danger to fingers. Before a run, the team leader checks that the machine is rated for the material and thickness, the clearance is set from the maker's chart, the blades are sharp and undamaged, the guards and hold-downs work, and the back gauge is set and checked by cutting and measuring a first-off part.
markingPoints: Correct clearance gives a clean edge; too large tears and burrs; too small wears blades
Rake lowers force but can twist narrow strips
Hold-downs keep the sheet still for a square, safe cut
Checks rating, clearance from the chart, blades, guards
Sets the back gauge and checks a first-off part

essays.stem: Describe a safe system for isolating a cutting machine to change a blade or clear a jam when more than one person will work on it. Include stored energy and proving.
essays.modelAnswer: First the job is planned and, where the Centre requires it, a permit is issued. The machine is stopped with its normal controls, and everyone who uses it is told it is being isolated. The main isolator is switched off. Because two or more people will work on it, a multi-lock hasp is fitted to the isolator and each person puts on their own padlock and a tag with their name. Nobody else holds their key. Stored energy is then dealt with: hydraulic pressure is released as the maker says, moving parts such as a bandsaw head or guillotine blade are lowered or blocked, springs are released and blades are allowed to stop. The isolation is then proved by pressing the start button with everyone clear: the machine must not run, and the controls are returned to off. Only then does the work start. When the job is finished, guards are refitted, tools removed and people stand clear. Each person removes only their own lock, and the machine is tested before it goes back into use.
markingPoints: Plans the job, tells users and switches off at the isolator
Multi-lock hasp: each person fits their own lock and tag
Releases or blocks stored energy (hydraulic, gravity, springs, moving blades)
Proves isolation by trying to start, then returns controls to off
Refits guards; each removes only their own lock; tests before use

essays.stem: Explain how you would choose a bandsaw blade and set the speed and feed for cutting (a) solid mild steel bar, (b) thin-wall tube and (c) stainless steel bar.
essays.modelAnswer: The blade pitch must suit the thickness of metal in the cut, so that several teeth are cutting at once but the gullets do not fill up with chips. For solid mild steel bar, which is a long cut, a coarser pitch is used so that each gullet can carry its chips out, with a bi-metal blade, a normal speed from the maker's chart and a steady feed with coolant. For thin-wall tube, the wall is only a few millimetres thick, so a finer pitch, often a variable-pitch blade, is used so that teeth do not snag and strip on the thin wall; the feed is kept light so the tube is not crushed, and it is clamped so it cannot spin. For stainless steel bar, a bi-metal blade made for hard materials is used, with a lower blade speed to keep heat down, but a firm, steady feed so the teeth cut and do not rub, because rubbing work-hardens stainless. Plenty of coolant is used. In every case I check the maker's chart and the chips: thin, curled chips show good cutting, while blue or powdery chips show the settings need changing.
markingPoints: Pitch matched to the thickness of metal in the cut
Solid bar: coarser pitch, normal speed, steady feed, coolant
Thin-wall tube: finer or variable pitch, light feed, clamped securely
Stainless: suitable blade, slower speed, firm feed to avoid work-hardening, coolant
Uses the maker's chart and reads the chips to adjust

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up a quality check plan for a batch of 100 cut parts: first-off, in-process and final checks, the tools, the records, and what happens to parts that do not conform.
essays.modelAnswer: I start from the drawing and cutting list, and note the key features and their tolerances, such as length ±1 mm, squareness and hole positions. I choose suitable measuring tools, such as a steel rule or tape for lengths, a caliper for small sizes and an engineer's square for squareness, and I check that they are in good order. The first part cut is a first-off: it is measured fully, by the operator and a second person, and recorded before the batch is started. During the run, I set in-process checks, for example every tenth part, and after any blade change or reset of the stop, because blades wear and stops can move. At the end, a final check is done on a sample, and the parts are counted and their marks checked. All results are written on an inspection sheet with the date and names. A part that does not conform is labelled, set apart in a quarantine area and reported; the cause is found and put right before cutting goes on, and the supervisor decides whether it is reworked or scrapped.
markingPoints: Identifies key features and tolerances from the drawing
Chooses and checks suitable measuring tools
First-off check by two people before the run
In-process checks at set intervals and after changes; final check and count
Records results; non-conforming parts quarantined, reported and the cause fixed

essays.stem: Explain the health hazards from mechanical cutting work (noise, dust, coolant, manual handling and sharp edges), and how a team leader controls them.
essays.modelAnswer: Saws, guillotines, punches and especially abrasive cut-off saws are loud, and long exposure damages hearing for good, so machines are maintained, the loudest work is done away from others, hearing protection is worn and signs are put up. Abrasive cutting makes fine dust and fumes, especially from coated steel, so it is done with extraction or good ventilation, with respirators where needed, and the area is cleaned by vacuum, not by blowing. Soluble coolants can cause skin rashes and breathing problems when old or dirty, so the mix is kept right, the coolant is changed as the maker says, skin contact is kept low with gloves and barrier cream, and hands are washed. Steel bars and sheets are heavy and awkward, so lifts are planned, trolleys, roller stands and lifting clamps are used, and team lifts are directed by one person. Cut edges and burrs are sharp, so gloves are worn, edges are deburred, and offcuts are put straight in bins. The team leader briefs the team, checks PPE is worn and asks them to report any symptoms.
markingPoints: Noise: hearing damage; maintenance, separation, hearing protection
Dust and fumes: extraction, ventilation, respirators, vacuum cleaning
Coolant: dermatitis; correct mix, changing, gloves, washing
Manual handling: planned lifts, aids, team lifts
Sharp edges: gloves, deburring, tidy offcuts; leader briefs and checks

essays.stem: A trainee in your team will use the ironworker for the first time. Describe how you would train and supervise them.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the trainee has had the Centre's general machine safety induction and is wearing the right PPE: safety glasses, gloves suited to the task, safety boots and close-fitting clothing. I explain the parts of the ironworker: the punch station, the shear blades for flat bar and angle, the notcher, the guards, the stripper, the foot pedal and the emergency stop. I explain the hazards, mainly crushing and cutting of the fingers, flying slugs and offcuts, and the machine's capacity limits from its plate. I show how to check the punch and die are matched and tight, and how to set the stripper and guards. I then demonstrate a cut and a punch while they watch, explaining each step. Next they do the same with me beside them, and I correct them straight away if needed. I let them carry on under close supervision until I am sure they are competent, then sign their training record. I keep checking their work and give them only jobs within their skill for a while.
markingPoints: Checks induction and PPE first
Explains the machine's parts, controls and emergency stop
Explains the hazards and capacity limits
Demonstrates, then lets them practise under close supervision with feedback
Signs off when competent and records the training

essays.stem: Describe what a maintenance and fault log for the Centre's cutting machines should contain, and explain how a team leader uses it.
essays.modelAnswer: The log should have a page for each machine, with its name, number and location. It should list the routine checks and when they are due, such as daily guard and emergency stop checks, weekly coolant checks, and blade and lubrication checks, as the maker's instructions say. Each entry gives the date, what was done, the parts fitted, such as a new blade with its type and pitch, the settings, such as the guillotine clearance, and the name of the person. Faults are recorded with the date, what was found, who found it, whether the machine was tagged out of use, and what repair was done and by whom, with the date it was passed safe to use again. A team leader reads the log before using a machine, to check it is in date and has no open faults. They use it to plan blade changes and services before a big job, to spot repeat faults and to show the supervisor where spares or repairs are needed. It is also a record if there is an accident or inspection.
markingPoints: Machine details and routine checks with due dates
Entries record date, work done, parts, settings and name
Faults recorded with tag-out, repair and return to service
Leader checks the log before use and plans maintenance
Used to spot repeat faults and as a record for safety and inspection

practical1.title: Plan, cut and inspect a full set of parts for a steel frame from a cutting list
practical1.brief: As a team, use the drawing and cutting list the assessor gives you (for example a welding table frame: four 40 × 40 × 3 mm square tube legs, four mitred top rails, two angle cross rails and four flat-bar feet). First, write a cutting plan: group the parts by section, fit them onto the stock lengths you are given, allow for squaring and saw cuts, choose the machine for each group and say who does what. Show your working for the stock needed and the offcuts left. Set up the cold saw or bandsaw with a length stop and the head angle for the mitres, and cut the parts. Cut the feet on the guillotine or ironworker. Do a first-off check on each group before cutting the rest, and check every part at the end for length, angle and squareness. Deburr all parts and mark each with its part number. Record all checks on the inspection sheet and enter useful offcuts in an offcut register. Each member sets up and cuts at least one group while the assessor watches, and checks parts cut by another member. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the parts and papers are finished and the area is clean.
materials: Stock lengths of 40 × 40 × 3 mm square tube, 40 × 40 × 4 mm angle and 50 × 6 mm flat bar
Drawing and cutting list (from the assessor)
Cold saw or bandsaw with length stop and roller stands; guillotine or ironworker
Steel tape, steel rule, engineer's square, protractor or bevel gauge, caliper
Files or deburring tools, paint marker
Cutting plan, inspection sheet and offcut register
photos: The written cutting plan with the stock and offcut working
The saw set up with the length stop and roller stands
A mitre being cut, with the work clamped and PPE worn
All the cut and marked parts laid out against the cutting list
The completed inspection sheet and offcut register
checklist: Helped write a cutting plan that allows for squaring and saw cuts
Checked the machine, guards and blade before use
Set the length stop and saw angle correctly
Clamped the work and cut safely, keeping hands clear
Carried out a first-off check and recorded it
Parts within the tolerance on the drawing, deburred and marked
Checked another member's parts and recorded the result
Recorded offcuts and left the machines isolated, clean and tidy
safety: Check guards and emergency stops before use; isolate and lock off before changing blades or clearing jams
Wear safety glasses, hearing protection, safety boots and gloves suited to the task; keep gloves away from moving blades
Support long bars on roller stands; keep walkways clear
Never reach into the cutting area while a machine is running; keep hands clear of hold-downs
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Set up and run a production batch of sheared and punched bracket blanks, with inspection records
practical2.brief: As a team, produce a batch of 20 bracket blanks from 3 mm mild steel sheet or 50 × 6 mm flat bar to the drawing the assessor gives you (for example 100 mm × 50 mm, with two 12 mm holes and one corner cropped at 45°). First, plan the run: the machines, the order, the settings and who does what. Check the guillotine's rating and set the blade clearance from the maker's chart; check that the punch and die on the ironworker or punch press match the hole size and are tight. Work out the punching force for one hole and check it against the machine's rating. Set the back gauge and the punch stops, cut and punch a first-off blank, and get it checked by another member and the assessor. Then run the batch, checking every fifth blank, and deburr and stack the parts. Record the settings, the first-off result and each check on the inspection sheet, and label any blank that does not conform. Each member operates at least one machine while the assessor watches, and every member does some of the checks. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the batch and the papers are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 3 mm mild steel sheet or 50 × 6 mm flat bar, enough for 20 blanks and set-up
Drawing of the blank (from the assessor)

checklist: Took part in planning the run and the force calculation
Checked the machine ratings, guards, hold-downs and stripper before use
Isolated the machine before making any adjustment to blades or tools
Set the back gauge and stops so that the first-off blank was within tolerance
Fed the material safely, with hands clear of the blade and punch
Carried out and recorded checks during the run
Labelled and set apart any blank that did not conform
Left the machines isolated, clean and tidy, with offcuts and slugs in the right bins
safety: Only trained members operate the guillotine and ironworker, one operator per machine at a time
Isolate and lock off before setting clearance, changing punches or clearing jams
Keep fingers out of the hold-down and punch area; use the guards and stripper
Wear safety glasses, gloves, safety boots and hearing protection
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
